title: The Ramsey community number as a renormalization-group crossing
abstract: The Ramsey community number $r_k$ is the smallest size at which a network is better described by communities than by none, under a Bayesian detection rule. On the diamond hierarchical lattice we show that $r_k$ is an exact renormalization-group crossing: the block-model sufficient statistics obey a linear map with eigenvalues $\{bs,b\}$, the degree-corrected evidence density flows to $\ln K$ at a community fixed point, and $r_k$ is the generation at which the running evidence clears the detection threshold. Degree correction advances detection by two generations. We derive $r_k(b,s;q)$ in closed form for the whole family. Finally, placing on the lattice the Reichardt--Bornholdt community Hamiltonian -- whose ground state is the partition itself -- we find an exact community-ordered phase: below the ferromagnetic critical temperature the two hubs lock into opposite communities for any resolution $γ>0$, a staggered order that persists as $n\to\infty$. Allowing each nested sub-community its own label, the optimal partition is a hierarchy of $q_{\rm opt}\sim\sqrt{n}$ communities, so the number of Potts states that best describes the network grows with the network. This hierarchy orders thermally level by level, through a cascade of first-order transitions whose temperatures fall as $1/\ln q$, so every stable level persists as $n\to\infty$: the emergent partition is detectable, optimal, and thermodynamically ordered.
summary: This work establishes that the statistical concept of community detection, quantified by the Ramsey number, has a deep physical underpinning. By mapping network structure onto renormalization group flow and analyzing it with spin Hamiltonians, the authors prove that the detected community pattern is not merely an artifact but represents a genuine, thermodynamically ordered phase in the system.
main_problem: The paper determines when a network's community structure becomes an 'objective fact,' quantified by the Ramsey community number ($r_\kappa$), and establishes its thermodynamic stability.
main_result: The Ramsey community number is shown to be an exact renormalization-group crossing, and the optimal partition forms a persistent, thermodynamically ordered hierarchy of communities.
method: The analysis combines Bayesian model comparison (evidence ratio) with Renormalization Group (RG) techniques applied to lattice models and spin Hamiltonians.
model_or_system: The study uses the diamond hierarchical lattice structure and analyzes community ordering via a generalized Potts Hamiltonian, which is related to modularity maximization.
key_observables: Ramsey community number ($r_\kappa$), block-pair sufficient statistics eigenvalues ($\lambda_{	ext{vol}}, \lambda_{	ext{seam}}$), evidence density flow, and the critical temperatures ($T_c(q)$) for phase transitions.
important_parameters: The detection threshold $q$, lattice parameters $(b, s)$, and community depth/number ($q_{	ext{opt}} \sim \sqrt{n}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the exact nature of real-space decimation on the diamond lattice to map RG steps precisely.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction of the lattice, the flow of block densities towards a fixed point, and phase diagrams showing community order vs. temperature for different hierarchy depths.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining $r_\kappa$ via RG analysis on the diamond lattice to deriving closed-form expressions for $r_\kappa$, culminating in placing the structure into a thermodynamic framework using a Potts Hamiltonian to prove persistent, level-by-level ordering.
why_interesting: While focused on network science metrics, the rigorous application of RG flow and phase transition theory (Potts model) to determine intrinsic structural order provides powerful analogies for understanding emergent phases in complex quantum many-body systems or disordered quantum materials.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Starting from a single bond between the poles A, B (t = 0), each generation replaces every edge by b = 2 parallel paths of s = 2 edges, adding one interior vertex per path; iterating gives m = 4t edges and nt = (2 · 4t + 4)/3 nodes [Eq. (3)]. Node area ∝degree, so the two poles emerge as the permanent degree-2t hubs.

Figure 2: Diamond lattice G3 (nt = 44) with the self-similar bundle cut. Red: bundle 0 together with the poles A, B; teal: bundle 1; gold: the e12 = 2t = 8 seam edges, every one incident on a pole. Node area ∝degree, exposing the two degree-2t hubs.

Figure 3: (a) Log evidence of the bundle split versus generation (symlog scale). The degree-corrected model clears the detection threshold ln[q/(1−q)] (dotted, q = 0.99) at t = 3, giving rκ = n3 = 44; the plain model only at t = 5, rκ = n5 = 684. The lattice exists only at the discrete sizes nt, so the crossing—and hence rκ—is a generation index. (b) Renormalization-group flow of the block densities Eq. (9) to the community fixed point (uin, u×) = (K, 0) = (2, 0); the seam density decays geometrically as (λseam/λvol)t = (1/s)t

Figure 4: Exact community-ordered phase of the q = 2 Reichardt–Bornholdt model on the diamond. Order parameter −⟨σAσB⟩(hub anti-alignment: 1 when the two hubs occupy opposite communities). (a) Versus temperature at t = 6 (nt = 2732) for three resolutions γ: the community order switches off at the ferromagnetic critical temperature T FM c , essentially independent of γ. (b) As the lattice grows the transition sharpens into a step at T FM c ; below it the order is persistent, −⟨σAσB⟩→1 as n →∞. (c) The (γ, T) phase diagram: a community-ordered region for all γ > 0 below T FM c (dashed).

Figure 5: Hierarchical community structure with a growing number of states. (a) Modularity Q of the depth-d nested partition (q = 2d communities), Eq. (22), versus depth for three sizes; stars mark the optimum, which moves to finer resolution as n grows. (b) The optimal number of communities qopt = 2d⋆tracks √n (dashed), Eq. (23), over t ≤9.
